title: Meeting Joe on Magazine Street and his boyhood
summary: She met Joe in New Orleans, where he worked as a yard boy for a family that raised him, took up cornet after trombone, and courted her for four or five years before 1912. His parents were Virginia and Henry, a minister.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the horn: first instrument and the trombone

blocks.x: Mrs. Near Donaldsonville. Near Donaldsonville, just three miles from where I was born. But I didn't know him as children. We didn't come in contact with each other. But his mother worked at a place called Salzburg. That was a plantation. But Joe was born in Abin. And when he came to New Orleans as a boy...
Excuse me, do you remember just when he was born, his birth date? Yes. He was born in...
On December the 19th. Nineteen... Nineteen... Nineteen... Eighteen...
Eighty-five.

Eighty-five. Eighty-five. Eighty-five. Eighty-five. I'm just a few years younger than Joe. And we met when we was in New Orleans working. We met... He was working two doors from me, where I work. And he was working for some Jewish family. They raised him. He was there as a boy. He didn't know much about Conrad, but he was determined to learn. So he started rehearsing, practicing, and he did fairly well.
Do you know when he moved to the city? Did he tell you when he moved?
No, I don't know. I only know him after he came to New Orleans. And we were two doors from each other on Magazine Street working.
Was that the place near Second Street? Yeah, Magazine and Second.
I was on Second and he was on Magazine... He was on Magazine near Second.
Near Second.
Yes. And when I met him, he was quite a young man. We were both going along in the courtenayes, running around together and all.
How long did you know him before he was married about?
Before we married? Oh, well, I knew him about four or five years before we were married.
So he was in the city several years before 1912.

Oh, yes. We married in 1912. We married in 1912. He was in the city quite a long time. His mother had passed and as a boy he went there and he lived on premises. And they probably just took him like their own family. They raised him. He did like he wanted and he started rehearsing for music. Well, he went off on a little tour up above Donisonville and he was stranded as a boy. The man took a couple of boys. Did he play in coronet then? He was playing the coronet then. And then he got stranded. He didn't have anything. But he played too loud. The man took him off of, he was playing then first trambone. He started on the trambone. Yes, but he played too loud for the trambone and then they put him on the coronet. And then that's the time I met Joe. And after I met Joe, of course we went around a long time together. And he got to going around playing at different dances. And he used to play at these balls. He'd have balls and he'd play. And of course then he got so good he didn't want to work anymore. And we met and we married.
What kind of work had he been doing on that?

He had been doing just ordinary work. Yard boy, they used to call him then. They'd clean the yard around him. And he could get off any time he wanted. And he got off any time he wanted. And they were very good to him. Didn't pay much of a salary, but they raised him. They raised him.
His mother died when he was quite young then? Oh, before I met him.
I had never met his mother.
Did he ever say anything about his father? No, but his... Did he play any instrument or anything?

No, his father didn't. His father, he always told me his father was a minister. He was a minister? Yes. His mother was named Virginia. And his father was named Henry. But I didn't meet him until his mother had passed. That's when he was in New Orleans. And after I met him, and he began playing. And then we got quite chummy. And he began to get popular. They used to play on the trucks.
